title: Chunked Action Output SDK Playbook (draft)
body:
Purpose
---
This doc captures a working playbook for a chunked/partial streaming response format that unifies typed action (tool call) fragments and structured output inside the Hosted API SDKs. The intention is to provide SDK ergonomics that: reduce developer friction for tool integration, preserve low-latency streaming for UI experiences, and enable deterministic structured output validation for server-side consumers.

Problem statement
---
Teams building interactive features (chat UIs, copilots, extraction services) require:
- fast, incremental display of model text
- early invocation of external tools (search, web, function execution) before the full response is ready
- final structured output that can be parsed/validated reliably

Existing issues we've observed:
- SDKs either stream raw tokens (good for latency) or wait and return a final structured payload (good for correctness), rarely both elegantly
- Tool-calling semantics become awkward mid-stream: how should SDKs surface an action the model requested at t=200ms?
- Frontend teams hack around this by re-parsing human-readable signals from tokens; backend teams re-run post-processing to find intents — both fragile.

Goals (product + UX + engineering)
---
1) Define a compact, forward-compatible chunk format that mixes: partial text, typed action frames, and provisional structured fields.
2) Provide SDK primitives that are incremental-first: onChunk(handler), onAction(handler), onFinal(result) with clear guarantees.
3) Keep network/compute efficient: low overhead per chunk, small memory footprint, and compatible with existing streaming transports.
4) Make migration easy for existing Hosted API users: default to backwards compatible token stream, opt-in to structured frames.
5) Surface clear validation and retry semantics for tool calls requested mid-stream.

Design constraints and non-goals
---
- This doc focuses on the API surface and SDK ergonomics. It does not mandate internal runtime scheduling or kernel selection policies.
- We will not attempt to define a full JSON-schema language here; rather, we support simple typed fields + optional schema URLs.
- Security and auth for tool calls will rely on existing per-request model: call routing via policies, no new auth primitives.

Chunk format (sketch)
---
Chunks are newline-delimited frames. Each frame is prefixed with a 1-byte type token (ASCII letter) followed by a compact payload. Types: 
- T: text fragment (utf-8). Payload = raw text.
- A: action frame (base64-json safe). Payload = minimal action envelope.
- S: structured partial (base64-json safe). Payload = partial fields or diffs.
- E: error/diagnostic. Payload = human string.

Why this shape?
- Minimizes framing overhead for high-frequency text tokens.
- Allows simple streaming handlers (read byte, switch).
- Avoids repeated large JSON blobs when only a small structured field updates.

Action frame (A) envelope fields (compact):
- id: short action id (client-visible)
- name: action name (e.g., search, call_http, run_code)
- args_ref: either inline args or an opaque storage ref for large payloads
- invocation_hint: optional intent hash for deduping
- early: boolean flag indicating model expects action result mid-response
- required_by: optional token index or timestamp (best-effort)

SDK semantics for action frames
---
- onAction(action) -> used by clients to decide when to actually invoke external tool.
- If action.early == true, the SDK should:
  1) emit an action callback synchronously to application code (preferably in the UI thread).
  2) provide an actionHandle with methods: respond(result), fail(reason), postpone().
  3) when respond() is called, SDK will send a compact action-result frame back to the model (if requested) without breaking the token stream.
- SDK must ensure action ids are stable across reconnects for the same conversation.
- For server-side SDKs, default policy is to buffer action invocations for batching unless the application opts into low-latency immediate invocation.

Text frames (T) and partials (S)
---
- T frames stream raw text; SDK should provide an incremental renderer that preserves token boundaries.
- S frames carry structured fields (e.g., {score: 0.87} or {entities: [{name:\"ACME\"}]}) as diffs or replacements. SDK should merge structured partials into a provisional object and expose a validation hook.

OnFinal(result) contract
---
- After model completes, the server emits a final F frame containing the canonical structured output and metadata (latency, model_version, action_outcomes).
- SDK guarantees: onFinal is called after all onAction callbacks for actions with required_by <= final were triggered and resolved (if the model requested results).

Error handling patterns
---
- E frames are advisory; SDK should surface them to user code but not terminate the stream by default.
- If an action fails and model flagged it required, SDK should: 
  - surface error, allow app to call actionHandle.fail(), and optionally let SDK send a failure token back to model.
- Network reconnects: SDK must be able to resume from last acked chunk. Recommended: include a numeric monotonic chunk sequence in the stream headers.

SDK API ergonomics (JS + Python sketches)
---
JS (browser):
- const stream = client.chat.stream({model, prompt, schema: optionalSchemaUrl});
- stream.on('text', chunk => renderChunk(chunk));
- stream.on('action', async (action, handle) => {
    if (action.name === 'search') {
      const r = await localSearch(action.args_ref || action.args);
      await handle.respond({results: r.slice(0,5)});
    }
  });
- stream.on('partial', obj => mergeProvisional(obj));
- stream.on('final', (result) => commit(result));
- stream.on('error', e => console.warn(e));

Python (server):
- with client.stream_chat(...) as s:
    for frame in s:
        if frame.type == 'text':
            process(frame.text)
        elif frame.type == 'action':
            # default: queue for batch executor
            batcher.add(frame)
        elif frame.type == 'final':
            validate_and_store(frame.payload)

Ergonomic defaults we prefer
---
- Browser SDK: immediate action callbacks and optimistic UI; explicit handle.respond ensures app controls data sent back.
- Node/server SDK: default to buffered action execution (batching) with a low-latency path opt-in.
- All SDKs expose a small set of helpers: createActionHandler, schemaValidator, joinChunksAsText.

Backward compatibility and opt-in path
---
- Default behaviour for existing clients is unchanged: they receive a T-only token stream.
- New clients can pass header X-Redwood-Chunking: v1 to enable frame parsing.
- Server will allow mixed streams for a migration window (12 months recommended).

Telemetry and KPIs
---
Track per-route and per-model:
- average first-chunk latency (ms)
- time-to-first-action-observed (ms)
- action-to-response latency (ms) when action was required
- fraction of streams that contain action frames
- schema validation failure rate on final frames
- error frame frequency and distribution

Rollout proposal
---
Phase 0 (internal): implement chunk format in a staging runtime, wire up a Node SDK prototype, test against internal copilot demos.
Phase 1 (alpha): enable X-Redwood-Chunking header; opt-in for beta customers, collect telemetry.
Phase 2 (beta): stabilize frame schema, add Python and browser SDK support, introduce migration docs.
Phase 3 (GA): enable for public SDKs and document performance tradeoffs; deprecate legacy opt-in after further notice.

Open questions / tradeoffs
---
- Should action frames be signed or carry an integrity token when used in Private deployments? (security teams)
- How to encode very large args (multi-MB)? Inline vs storage ref — impacts latency and round trips.
- UX: when the model requests multiple actions with overlapping required_by windows, how do we present ordering guarantees?
- Diagnostics: what debugging hooks do we offer to surface partial merges when structured fields disagree?

Next steps (short-term)
---
- Spike: implement parser for prefix-type frames in the runtime (eng-serving-runtime) — owner: Marcus Lee — 2w.
- Prototype: Node SDK event model + sample copilot integration (devexp) — owner: Amaya Chen — 3w.
- Playtest: run with 3 internal teams (search, codegen, docs-assistant) to iterate UX — owner: Nora Patel — 4w.

Notes to reviewers
---
This is intentionally prescriptive but not normative. The goal is to converge on an ergonomic surface that keeps work off application teams while preserving low-level flexibility for advanced users. Please call out missing developer workflows, real-world action examples we should test, and any compliance constraints for private deployments.
